## Overview

The Hinukh (Hinukh: *гьинухъес hinuqes*; Avar: *гьинухъесел*, romanized *hinuqesel*) are a people of Dagestan living chiefly in Genukh, their “parent village” in Tsuntinsky District, and in Novomonastyrskoe, Kizlyarsky District, where they settled later among Avars and Dargins; others live in the cities of Dagestan. The 2021 Russian census registered 630 Hinukh, nearly all living in Dagestan, while the 2002 Russian Census recorded 531 and treated them as a subgroup of the Avar people. Their language belongs to the Northeast Caucasian family, within the Tsezic subgroup, and is closely related to Tsez. The sources are significant for folk-culture research because they document a small community undergoing assimilation by Caucasian Avars, alongside a distinctive language, oral naming traditions, and a history of changing official classification.

## Music & performance

The available material does record that Hinukh language preservation is connected with ethnographic and folkloristic work: Aleksandr Serzhputovkiy provided a list of 16 Hinukh words with their Tsez counterparts in a work about the Tsez people in 1916.

## Festivals & rituals

The Hinukh are overwhelmingly Sunni Muslims. They converted to Islam possibly in the late 18th century through mountain guides from the Free Community of Gidatl and Khunzakh and through the Bezhta people, who were already Muslims.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Hinukh people were already mentioned in the Georgian chronicles of the Early Middle Ages. The sources also preserve several historical acts of linguistic documentation: the first written material about Hinukh was a list of 16 words with Tsez counterparts given by Aleksandr Serzhputovkiy in 1916; the language itself was first described in 1916 by Russian ethnographer A. Serzhputovsky; and the first information about Archi language appeared in a letter from Peter von Uslar to Franz Anton Schiefner dated 1865, concerning a special language in Inukho aul, identified as Hinukh.

## Language & religion

The Hinuq language, also known as Hinukh, Hinux, Ginukh, or Ginux, has the autonym *гьинузас мец hinuzas mec*. It is a Northeast Caucasian language of the Tsezic subgroup, spoken by about 200 to 500 people in southwestern Dagestan, mainly in Genukh, called *Hino* in Hinukh. Hinukh is very closely related to Tsez but is not entirely mutually intelligible with it. Only half of the children of the village speak Hinukh, and because the language is unwritten, Avar and Russian serve as literary languages. Many Hinukh also speak Avar, Tsez, Russian, and often other languages of the region. Linguists have variously classified Hinukh as an independent language or as a dialect of Tsez; Nicholas Marr described it as a language “between Avar and Dido languages,” while D.S. Imnaishvili and E.S. Lomtadze classified it as a Tsez dialect.

Hinukh has six vowel qualities, six diphthongs, voiced and unvoiced consonants, ejectives, and consonant gemination. Its stems may have the structures CV, CV:, or CVC, while inflected words may also have CV:C and CVyC structures. It is an agglutinative language that mainly uses suffixes and an ergative-absolutive language with singular and plural number. It has six non-spatial cases and 35 spatial cases, organized through location and orientation markers. Verbs can express tense, aspect, mood, evidentiality, polarity, illocutionary force, gender, and number. Hinuq has five grammatical genders, five simple tenses, and 14 complex tenses. Its numeral system is vigesimal, or base-20.
